- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.text: Design fully validated empirically. Writing up.

input.approach_name: Clojure-style bit-partitioned vector trie with always-Branch root, lazy 32-element tail, and pre-collected leaf-slice iteration (validated prototype at /tmp/proto/src/pvec.rs)
input.data_structure:
Chosen: FULL RECURSIVE TRIE (Option A). Rejected the "leaves-only flat Vec<Rc<[T;32]>> spine" (Option B) — see pitfalls; I benchmarked it and it is quadratic (148 -> 670 -> 3503 ns/push at n = 100k/400k/1.6M) because every tail flush must clone the whole spine Vec, and it is not structurally shared.

    const BITS: u32 = 5; const WIDTH: usize = 32; const MASK: usize = 31;

    enum Node<T> {
        Branch(Vec<Rc<Node<T>>>),  // 0..=32 children, LEFT-PACKED (no gaps, no None slots)
        Leaf(Vec<T>),              // ALWAYS exactly 32 elements
    }

    pub struct PVec<T> {
        cnt: usize,         // total size
        shift: u32,         // level of root; >= 5, multiple of 5. Leaves live at level 0.
        root: Rc<Node<T>>,  // ALWAYS a Branch; holds exactly tail_off elements
        tail: Rc<Vec<T>>,   // 0..=32 elements
    }

Derived (never stored, so they cannot desynchronize):
  tail_off() = cnt - tail.len()      // index of first tail element; always a multiple of 32
  leaf_cnt() = m = tail_off() >> 5   // number of leaves in the tree

Two representation choices do all the correctness work:
1. Root is ALWAYS a Branch at shift >= 5, even for the empty vector (`Branch(Vec::new())`, which does not heap-allocate). This removes every special case from the descent loop: there is no "root is a bare leaf at depth 1" case, and no Option<root>.
2. Branch children are a left-packed `Vec`, so `children.len()` IS the count of populated slots. This is what makes the push_tail case analysis a two-way `sub == len` vs `sub < len` test with no separate occupancy bookkeeping.

Clone is hand-written (Rc::clone of root+tail, copy cnt/shift) so it does not require T: Clone; only push_back needs T: Clone. Default is hand-written for the same reason.
key_invariants: I1 (tail bounds): tail.len() <= 32, and tail.len() == 0 if and only if cnt == 0. Equivalently tail.len() in [1,32] whenever cnt >= 1.

I2 (tail offset): tail_off = cnt - tail.len() is always a multiple of 32, and for cnt > 0 it equals ((cnt-1) >> 5) << 5. This second form is a redundant cross-check and is asserted in audit(); it holds only because the tail is flushed LAZILY.
I3 (tree holds the prefix): the tree stores exactly elements [0, tail_off) as m = tail_off >> 5 full leaves; the tail stores [tail_off, cnt).

I4 (leaves are full): every Node::Leaf in the tree has exactly 32 elements. True because a leaf is only ever created from a tail that had reached exactly 32. This is what makes chunked iteration and `chunk[i & 31]` unconditional.
I5 (shift shape): shift >= 5 and shift % 5 == 0; root is a Branch; leaves sit at level 0; every root-to-leaf path has exactly shift/5 branch levels (uniform depth).
I6 (capacity): a subtree rooted at level s addresses at most (1 << s) leaves = (1 << (s+5)) elements. Global: m <= (1 << shift).
I7 (shift minimality): shift == 5, or m > (1 << (shift - 5)). I.e. we never carry a taller tree than needed, so depth is a function of size alone and index math is canonical.

I8 (left-packed / no gaps): for a subtree at level s holding `want` leaves with C = 1 << (s-5) leaves per child, children.len() == ceil(want / C), children[0..len-1] are each exactly full (C leaves), and only the LAST child may be partial. Elements are dense from index 0.

I9 (persistence): push_back mutates nothing reachable from self. Every node on the modified root-to-leaf path is freshly allocated; all other children are Rc::clone'd. Older PVec values remain valid and observationally unchanged forever.
I10 (index routing): for i < cnt, i >= tail_off routes to the tail, i < tail_off routes to the tree; these are exhaustive and disjoint.
input.index_algorithm:
get(&self, i: usize) -> Option<&T>:
    if i >= self.cnt { return None; }               // the ONLY bounds check; covers cnt == 0
    Some(&self.chunk_for(i)[i & 31])

chunk_for(&self, i: usize) -> &[T]      // returns the 32-wide chunk (or tail) containing i
    if i >= self.tail_off() { return &self.tail; }   // tail hit
    let mut node: &Node<T> = &self.root;
    let mut s = self.shift;                          // shift == 5 * (number of branch levels)
    while s > 0 {
        node = &node.children()[(i >> s) & 31];
        s -= 5;
    }
    node.leaf()                                      // s reached 0 -> we are at a Leaf

Index<usize> for PVec delegates to get(i).expect("index out of bounds").

RADIX ARITHMETIC, exactly:
  - Level s addresses a span of (1 << (s+5)) elements; its child j covers
    [j << (s+5), (j+1) << (s+5)).
  - The digit selecting the child at level s is (i >> s) & 31.
  - The loop visits s = shift, shift-5, ..., 5 (that is 5*(depth-1) down to 5), then stops at s == 0
    where the node is a Leaf and the final digit is (i >> 0) & 31 == i & 31.
  - Because leaves are always exactly 32 wide (I4) and the tree is dense (I8), the child index
    produced at every level is < children.len(); no bounds violation is reachable for i < tail_off.

BOUNDARY CASES (all confirmed by running the prototype and auditing every invariant at each size;
"leaves" = m, i.e. leaves actually in the tree):

  cnt      shift  leaves(m)  tail  notes
  0        5      0          0     root = Branch([]). get(anything) -> None. No tree walk ever runs.
  31       5      0          31    tail_off = 0, so EVERY index routes to the tail.
  32       5      0          32    KEY: the tail is NOT flushed at 32. The tree is still empty even
                                   though size is 32. get(31) -> tail[31 & 31] = tail[31].
  33       5      1          1     Push #33 flushed the 32-tail as leaf 0. root = Branch([Leaf32]).
                                   tail_off = 32. get(32) -> tail[0]; get(31) -> tree: (31>>5)&31 = 0
                                   -> children[0], leaf[31].
  1023     5      31         31    tail_off = 992.
  1024     5      31         32    == 32*32. The tree holds only 992 elements; the last 32 are in the
                                   tail. get(1023) -> tail[31]; get(991) -> (991>>5)&31 = 30 ->
                                   children[30], leaf[31]. Depth has NOT grown.
  1025     5      32         1     "1024+1". Push #1025 flushed leaf 31 -> root now has all 32 leaf
                                   children (1024 elements) and is EXACTLY FULL (m == 32 == 1<<5),
                                   which is legal under I6. shift is STILL 5 -- no depth growth here.
                                   get(1024) -> tail[0]; get(1023) -> children[31], leaf[31].
  1056     5      32          32   tree full AND tail full: the next push must grow.
  1057     10     33          1    DEPTH-GROWTH BOUNDARY. m was 32 >= 1<<5, so
                                   root = Branch([old_root@5, new_path(5, leaf32) = Branch([leaf32])])
                                   at shift 10. Re-verify: get(1024) -> (1024>>10)&31 = 1 ->
                                   children[1] -> (1024>>5)&31 = 32&31 = 0 -> children[0] = leaf32 ->
                                   leaf32[1024 & 31] = leaf32[0]. Correct. get(1023) -> (1023>>10)&31
                                   = 0 -> old_root -> (1023>>5)&31 = 31 -> leaf31[31]. Correct.
  32768    10     1023        32   == 32^3. Again the tail holds the last 32; tree has 32736.
  32800    10     1024        32   tree exactly full at shift 10 (1024 leaves) AND tail full.
  32801    15     1025        1    next depth growth. General rule: growth happens at element number
                                   32*((1 << shift) + 1) + 1  ->  1057, 32801, 1048577, ...

  The "n-th push grows the trie" formula 32*((1<<shift)+1)+1 is the one thing most re-implementations
  get wrong by 32 (they grow at 1025). Growing at 1025 still produces correct indices, but it breaks
  I7 (shift minimality) and then every later boundary drifts.
module_layout: /output/Cargo.toml -- [package] name/version, edition = "2021"; NO [dependencies] section at all. Optionally [profile.release] to keep it boring. (Layout also builds with a bare `rustc --edition 2021 -O src/main.rs`, since `mod pvec;` resolves to src/pvec.rs; do not rely on cargo being the entry point.)

/output/src/main.rs -- `mod pvec; use pvec::PVec;` plus: stoi() emulation, argv handling (default 11), the two build/sum loops using i32 wrapping arithmetic, two println!. Nothing about the trie lives here.

/output/src/pvec.rs -- the whole data structure, in this order so it reads as a proof: consts BITS/WIDTH/MASK; enum Node with children()/leaf() accessors that panic on the unreachable arm; struct PVec; hand-written Clone and Default; len/is_empty/tail_off/leaf_cnt; get/chunk_for + impl Index<usize>; free fns new_path and push_tail; impl<T: Clone> PVec::push_back; collect_leaves + iter + struct Iter + Iterator/ExactSizeIterator + IntoIterator for &PVec; impl FromIterator (convenience); pub fn audit() -> Result<(), String> checking I1-I8 including a recursive left-packed/uniform-depth walk.

/output/src/pvec/tests.rs (or a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` block at the bottom of pvec.rs) -- (1) a deliberately naive `Oracle<T>{ v: Vec<T> }` whose push_back clones the whole Vec: this is the Option-B-style trivially-correct model; (2) differential test asserting len, every index, full iter output, and audit() for EVERY size 0..4200 (crosses 32, 1024, 1056, 1057); (3) large-n spot checks at 32768/32800/32801/1048577; (4) a persistence test that retains all 3000 snapshots and re-audits and re-reads each one; (5) empty-vector iteration; (6) a String (non-Copy) instantiation.

NOTE: a complete, compiling, fully-passing reference implementation of exactly this design already exists at /tmp/proto/src/pvec.rs (structure + audit) and /tmp/proto/src/main.rs (stoi + oracle + the whole test battery + a boundary-table dumper reachable via `--selftest`). It builds warning-free with rustc 1.75.0 and its output is byte-identical to /workspace/dataset/test11_executable on 33 values of n and 9 argument edge cases. Copy from there rather than retyping the index/push math.
pitfalls: i32 WRAPPING IS OBSERVABLE. `sum` and `v[i]*2` are C++ `int`. The reference wraps: n=65536 prints -2147450880 / 65536; n=1048576 prints 524288 / 1048576. Use i32 with wrapping_add / wrapping_mul. Plain `+`/`*` panics in a debug build and, worse, a u64/i64 accumulator silently prints the wrong number.

DO NOT FLUSH THE TAIL EAGERLY. The 32nd push must leave the tree empty and the tail at 32; the flush happens on push #33. Eager flushing makes tail.len() == 0 with cnt == 32, which breaks I1 and the tail_off = ((cnt-1)>>5)<<5 identity, and then every subsequent boundary is off by 32.

GROWTH CONDITION: test the LEAF COUNT against capacity (m >= 1 << shift), not the element count against 1 << (shift+5). The 32 elements sitting in the tail make the element-count form off by one level. Growth fires when pushing element 1057, NOT 1025. At size 1025 the shift-5 root is exactly full (32 leaf children) and that is legal.

new_path LEVEL ARGUMENT: the root-growth arm calls new_path(shift, leaf) (the new subtree is a SIBLING of the old root, so it lives at the old root's level); the push_tail arm calls new_path(shift - 5, leaf) (a CHILD). Swapping these produces a tree that indexes correctly for the first 1056 elements and then silently returns wrong values -- so any test that stops at 1024 will not catch it.

OPTION B (flat Vec<Rc<chunk>> spine) IS QUADRATIC AND NOT PERSISTENT-SHARED. I implemented and measured it: 148 / 670 / 3503 ns per push at n = 100k / 400k / 1.6M (4x time per 4x n), because each of the n/32 flushes clones a spine of average length n/64. Retaining snapshots would cost O(n^2/32) pointers. It also fails the task's "genuine structurally-shared trie" requirement. Keep it ONLY as the #[cfg(test)] oracle.

ITERATOR next() MUST USE `while`, NOT `if`, when advancing past a chunk boundary -- or you must guarantee no zero-length chunk is ever in `chunks` (which the design does, by only pushing the tail when non-empty). An `if` plus an empty chunk silently truncates iteration.

DO NOT reach for Rc::make_mut / Rc::get_mut on the tail to avoid the clone. push_back takes &self, so self's Rc keeps strong_count >= 2 for any clone you make; make_mut therefore always copies anyway (correct but pointless), and if you ever contrive a count of 1 you would mutate a tail that an older snapshot still shares, silently corrupting persistence.

Node accessor helpers must panic loudly (`unreachable!`) on the wrong variant, never unwrap_unchecked. The case analysis proves those arms are dead; a safe panic turns a proof error into a test failure instead of UB.

DO NOT #[derive(Clone)] or #[derive(Default)] on PVec<T> -- derive adds a spurious `T: Clone` / `T: Default` bound. Hand-write both. Keep `T: Clone` confined to the impl block that holds push_back so get/iter/len work for any T.

shift - BITS underflow: push_tail must only ever be entered with shift >= 5, and its recursive arm only with shift > 5. Both are provable (the s == 5 case always takes the ch.push arm), but assert them; a u32 underflow here becomes a gigantic shift and a panic far from the cause.

`v = v.push_back(i + 1)` DOES compile under NLL (the borrow ends when push_back returns, before the assignment) -- I verified it. Do not contort the API into a consuming `fn push_back(self, ...)` to dodge a borrow error that does not exist; that would change the persistence semantics the task is testing.

stoi fidelity, if the harness checks stderr/exit codes: skip leading whitespace, accept one +/-, consume decimal digits, IGNORE trailing garbage ("12abc" -> 78/156, " 7" -> 28/56, "0x10" -> 0). No digits at all (including an empty arg) -> invalid_argument; magnitude beyond i32 -> out_of_range. Both abort with SIGABRT (shell rc 134) after printing EXACTLY, on stderr: "terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::invalid_argument'\n  what():  stoi\n" (two spaces before `what()`, two after the colon). Use eprintln! + std::process::abort(). Verified byte-identical.

The empty vector's root is Rc::new(Node::Branch(Vec::new())) -- Vec::new does not heap-allocate, so this costs one Rc header and buys away every special case in chunk_for. Resist "optimizing" it into an Option<Rc<Node>> or allowing a bare-Leaf root; that reintroduces the depth-1 special case that is the usual source of index bugs.

Test the SIZES, not just the values. A test loop that only reaches n = 1000 exercises zero depth growths and would pass with a completely wrong growth rule. The differential test must cross 32, 1024, 1056/1057 and at least spot-check 32800/32801.

Fine but unnecessary, do not bother: usize::ilog2 (1.67) and usize::next_power_of_two for computing shift -- deriving shift incrementally in push_back is simpler and keeps I7 obviously maintained. let-else (1.65) is available if you want it.

rustc invoked directly with -O turns cfg(debug_assertions) OFF, so all the debug_assert!s and the audit() cross-checks cost the shipped binary nothing; pass -C debug-assertions=on explicitly for the verification build. If the harness uses `cargo build` with no --release, debug_assertions are ON -- which is exactly why the i32 arithmetic must be wrapping_* rather than plain operators.

Recursion depth in new_path / push_tail / collect_leaves is bounded by shift/5 <= 12 on 64-bit (usize::MAX elements) and <= 6 on 32-bit, so no stack-overflow risk and no need for an explicit stack. collect_leaves recurses on depth, not on n.

`1usize << shift` is safe for every reachable shift (<= 60 on 64-bit); it would only overflow at shift >= 64, which requires more than 2^64 elements. On a 32-bit target shift maxes out near 30 -- still fine, but the capacity comparison must be usize (not u32) so it does not truncate.
